sections.text:
The book opens with a death and an order. “Moses my servant is dead.” The leader is gone, and the LORD speaks to Joshua: arise, cross the Jordan, take this people into the land. The same charge comes back again and again: “Be strong and courageous.”

The first half of the book tells how Israel entered the land of Canaan: the crossing of the Jordan, the fall of Jericho and a series of campaigns (chapters 1 to 12). The second half divides the land among the tribes (13 to 22).

The last scene is at Shechem. Joshua gathers the tribes and puts a choice to them: “choose today whom you will serve”. Then he says where he stands: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” The people answer that they will serve the LORD too, and the covenant is renewed.

The book names no author and its date is debated. How its account relates to the findings of archaeology is also debated among scholars. The book is named for its main figure, and Joshua’s name is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus.

The warfare in this book raises hard questions, and Christians do not treat it as a model for violence. Some read the commands as a unique act of judgment at one moment in the history of salvation. Others point out that ancient war accounts used sweeping language, and that the book itself shows Canaanites such as Rahab being spared and many peoples remaining.

Hebrews 4 reads the rest that Joshua gave as pointing to a greater rest still to come.

Moses my servant is dead. Joshua hears the news and the command in the same breath: now arise, go across this Jordan. The LORD gives him the land from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates and the great sea, and promises that no one will stand before him all his life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you.

Three times the LORD says it: be strong and courageous. Joshua is to keep all the law Moses commanded, not turning right or left. The book of the law is not to depart from his mouth, and he is to meditate on it day and night. The LORD is with him wherever he goes.

Joshua then moves. He tells the officers to tell the people to prepare food, for in three days they cross. To the Reubenites, the Gadites and half of Manasseh, who settled east of the Jordan, he recalls what Moses said: your fighting men must cross armed and help their brothers.

They answer that they will go wherever he sends them, as they listened to Moses.

Joshua opens the section of the Bible often called the Former Prophets, which tells Israel's story from the land to the exile. The speaker is Joshua's new commander, the LORD, and the setting is the east bank of the Jordan after the long wilderness years. The words to be strong and courageous echo Deuteronomy 31. Joshua is described as Moses' servant, and the promise of the land goes back to Genesis 15. The tribes east of the Jordan are described in Numbers 32.

Two spies slip into Jericho and end up in the house of a prostitute named Rahab. The king hears of it and sends word to bring them out. Rahab has already hidden them under stalks of flax on her roof, and she tells the king's men that the strangers left at dusk and could still be caught.

Then she goes up to the roof and speaks to the spies. She has heard how the LORD dried up the Red Sea and what happened to Sihon and Og. Our hearts melted, she says, for the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on earth beneath. She asks them to swear to spare her father's house, since she dealt kindly with them.

They agree, and she lowers them by a cord through her window in the city wall. They give her a sign: a scarlet thread tied in the window, and everyone in her house must stay inside.

She ties it. The spies hide in the hills for three days and then report to Joshua that all the inhabitants melt away before them.

Rahab is an outsider who shows faith in the God of Israel. She appears again in Joshua 6, and the New Testament mentions her as an ancestor of Jesus in Matthew 1, and as an example of faith in Hebrews 11 and of works in James 2. Christians have read her lie to the king in different ways, and the text itself does not comment on it. Many readers see her story as a sign that outsiders could join Israel.

Joshua rises early, and Israel camps by the Jordan, in the season when the river overflows all its banks. After three days the officers pass through the camp with instructions. When you see the ark of the covenant carried by the Levitical priests, leave your place and follow, keeping a space of about two thousand cubits, so that you will know the way, for you have not passed this way before.

Joshua tells the people to sanctify themselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders. The LORD tells Joshua that today he will begin to magnify him, so Israel will know that as he was with Moses, he will be with Joshua.

The priests carry the ark to the water's edge. As soon as their feet touch the river, the water coming down from above stands in one heap, far upstream at Adam, and the water below is cut off. The priests stand firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan while all Israel crosses over, near Jericho, until the whole nation has passed.

The crossing recalls the Red Sea in Exodus 14, and the next chapter says so directly. The ark is the symbol of the LORD's presence, and the people follow it as their guide. A twelve-man group, one from each tribe, is chosen in verse 12 and appears again in chapter 4. Some readers have noted that the damming of a river at the town of Adam has parallels in history, but the text describes the event as the LORD's act.

When all the nation has crossed, the LORD tells Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each tribe. Each is to take a stone from the middle of the Jordan, from the place where the priests' feet stood firm, and carry it to the camp for the night.

Joshua explains. When your children ask in the future, What do you mean by these stones? you will tell them how the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant. They are a memorial forever.

The twelve do it. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the river, where the priests stood. The priests wait until everything is done, and then at the LORD's command they come up, and the waters return to their place and overflow the banks as before.

On the tenth day of the first month, Israel camps at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones there. He repeats the lesson for the children: the LORD dried up the Jordan as he did the Red Sea, so that all peoples may know his hand is mighty.

The stones are an early example of memory built into the landscape, and the question of the children echoes Exodus 12 and 13 and Deuteronomy 6. Gilgal becomes a base for Israel's early camps and appears in later chapters and in 1 Samuel. The date, the tenth day of the first month, falls four days before Passover, which the next chapter describes. About forty thousand armed men are mentioned in verse 13.

The kings across the land hear that the Jordan was dried up, and their hearts melt. Israel stands at the edge of the first fight, and the LORD tells Joshua to stop and make flint knives. The generation born in the wilderness was never circumcised, and the sign of the covenant is now renewed. When it is done, they rest in the camp until they are healed.

The LORD says, Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you, and the place is called Gilgal. They keep the Passover on the fourteenth day, in the plains of Jericho, and the next day they eat the produce of the land. The manna stops. After forty years, the people eat the fruit of Canaan.

Then Joshua looks up near Jericho and sees a man standing with a drawn sword. Are you for us, or for our enemies? he asks. No, the man says, I have come as commander of the LORD's army. Joshua falls on his face and worships. Take off your sandals, the man says, for the place where you stand is holy.

The scene with the commander echoes Moses at the burning bush in Exodus 3. The man's answer shows that the LORD is not on anyone's side so much as Israel is called to be on his. Many readers see the figure as an angel or as a visit of the LORD himself, and the text leaves it open. The manna began in Exodus 16, and its end marks a change of life. The circumcision rule goes back to Genesis 17.

Jericho is shut up tight. No one goes out, no one comes in. The LORD tells Joshua his plan, and it is not a siege. The soldiers are to march around the city once a day for six days, with seven priests carrying seven rams' horn trumpets before the ark. On the seventh day they march seven times, the priests blow, and the people shout, and the wall will fall down flat.

Joshua gives the order, and the people must say nothing until he tells them to shout. For six days the trumpets sound and the army circles in silence. On the seventh, at dawn, they go around seven times. Then Joshua says, Shout, for the LORD has given you the city!

The wall falls. The city is devoted to the LORD, and everything that breathes in it is destroyed. Only Rahab and those in her house are saved, as the spies swore, and she lives in Israel to this day. Joshua lays a curse on anyone who rebuilds the city, and his fame spreads through the land.

This chapter contains one of the hardest ideas in the Bible, the devoting of a city to destruction. Readers differ widely on how to understand it. Some see the language as ritual and exaggerated, as in similar ancient accounts, and some see it as a real act that Christians and Jews have found painful, and the text should not be used to justify violence today. The story of Rahab in chapter 2 stands next to it. Hebrews 11 recalls the fall of the wall as a work of faith.

Joshua's army had just seen a wall fall, and now they lose a small battle. Israel sends about three thousand men against Ai, and they flee. Thirty-six are killed, and the hearts of the people melt and become like water.

Joshua tears his clothes and lies on his face before the ark until evening, with dust on his head. Why, Lord GOD, did you bring us over the Jordan at all? he asks. What will you do for your great name? The LORD tells him to get up. Israel has sinned. Someone has taken some of the devoted things from Jericho, hidden them among his own goods, and Israel cannot stand until it is removed.

The next morning the lot narrows from tribe to family to household to man, and Achan is taken. Joshua asks him to confess. He says he saw a beautiful robe, silver and a wedge of gold, coveted them and buried them in his tent. They are found there. Achan and his family are brought to the valley of Achor and stoned, and a heap of stones is raised over him.

This is one of the hardest stories in Joshua. It shows a belief that the guilt of one person could affect the whole community, an idea that appears in Deuteronomy 24 along with the rule that children are not to die for their fathers, and readers have long asked how the two fit together. The text does not say whether Achan's family knew, and some readers note that the verbs in verse 25 are ambiguous. Joshua 8 continues with Ai.

Israel has just failed at Ai, and now the word comes again: “Don’t be afraid, and don’t be dismayed.” This time there is a plan. Joshua sends thirty thousand men out by night to hide behind the city, then marches up with the rest of the people and makes camp in front of it.

When the king of Ai sees them, he and his men rush out. Joshua and Israel pretend to be beaten and run toward the wilderness, and every man in Ai and Bethel follows. Joshua stretches out his javelin, the hidden men rise, take the empty city and set it on fire. The pursuers turn around and see smoke climbing the sky, with Israel on both sides of them.

After the city falls, Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and writes a copy of Moses’ law on stones. The people stand on two mountains while he reads aloud the blessing and the curse, women, children and foreigners among them.

Joshua leads Israel in the land of Canaan, and this chapter follows the defeat at Ai told in chapter 7. The battle is described in the harsh terms of devoted destruction, a theme that runs through the first half of the book. Jews and Christians have read such passages in different ways, and how they relate to history is debated by scholars. The ceremony on Ebal and Gerizim fulfills a command given through Moses; see Deuteronomy 27 and 11. Chapter 9 turns to the nations’ response.

Word of Jericho and Ai travels fast, and kings across the land gather to fight Israel. The people of Gibeon choose another way. They load their donkeys with worn sacks and torn wineskins, put on patched sandals and old clothes, and carry bread that is dry and moldy.

At Gilgal they tell Joshua they have come from a far country because of the LORD’s fame, and they ask for a covenant. The men of Israel sample their food. The text says plainly that they “didn’t ask counsel from the LORD’s mouth.” Joshua makes peace, and the leaders swear an oath.

Three days later the truth comes out: these are neighbors. The people of Israel grumble, but the leaders hold to what they swore. Joshua confronts the Gibeonites, who answer that they were afraid for their lives. They are spared, and made wood cutters and water carriers for the altar.

This chapter sits between the fall of Ai and the great battle at Gibeon in chapter 10. Gibeon was a sizable city not far from Israel’s camp. The story shows how seriously an oath sworn in the LORD’s name was taken, even when it was gained by deceit. Later parts of the Bible return to Gibeon; see 2 Samuel 21 for how the oath was remembered generations afterward. Readers often notice the contrast between Israel’s skill in war and its blind spot in a quiet conversation.

The king of Jerusalem is afraid. Gibeon has made peace with Israel, and Gibeon is a great city. He calls four other kings to his side, and the five armies camp against Gibeon. The Gibeonites send word to Joshua: “Don’t abandon your servants!”

Joshua marches all night from Gilgal and comes on the enemy suddenly. The text says the LORD confused them and hurled great stones from the sky as they fled. Then Joshua speaks to the LORD before all Israel: “Sun, stand still on Gibeon!” The text says the sun stayed in the middle of the sky for about a whole day, and that no day was like it before or after. It points readers to the book of Jashar.

The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah and are later put to death. The rest of the chapter lists city after city that falls, and Joshua returns to Gilgal.

This is the center of the book’s account of the southern campaign. The language of total destruction is hard to read, and the text itself says the LORD fought for Israel. Jews and Christians have understood these passages in different ways, and many have warned against using them to justify violence today. How to understand the day the sun stayed has been discussed for centuries; some read it as a literal event, others as poetry, and the book of Jashar is quoted as a source. See also Habakkuk 3.

Now the north rises. Jabin king of Hazor sends messages to kings near and far, and they come out with their armies, a host “many people, even as the sand that is on the seashore in multitude”, with horses and chariots beyond counting. They meet at the waters of Merom.

The LORD tells Joshua not to be afraid and promises that by the same time tomorrow they will be defeated. He also gives a strange command: hamstring the horses and burn the chariots. Joshua attacks suddenly and does exactly that. Then he turns back to Hazor, the head of all those kingdoms, and burns it.

The chapter closes with a summary. Joshua made war a long time, and apart from the Hivites of Gibeon no city made peace. The text says he left nothing undone of what Moses was commanded, and the land had rest from war.

The chapter completes the picture of the conquest begun in chapter 6: first the center, then the south, now the north. The command to disable the horses and chariots shows what Israel was meant to lean on; compare Psalm 20. The harsh language about killing everyone has troubled readers for a long time, and scholars and traditions differ over how it relates to history and how it should be read today. Many have said it can never be used as a pattern for violence in later times.

After pages of battle, the book pauses and counts. This chapter is a list, a kind of scorecard, but it reads like a roll call of everything that came before.

First come the two kings east of the Jordan whom Moses and Israel defeated: Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan, whose land was given to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. Then comes the longer list, king after king west of the Jordan, from the king of Jericho and the king of Ai to the king of Hazor and the king of Tirzah. Each is named with the same plain refrain, “one.”

The total is given at the end: thirty-one kings. A reader who has followed the campaign sees the names again, and the chapter works like a memorial of what Israel believed the LORD had done.

The list comes right before the second half of the book, where the land is divided among the tribes. Lists like this were a normal way for ancient writers to close a section and fix its record in memory. Readers often skim them, but each name was a real place that later chapters pick up again. Compare the earlier accounts of Sihon and Og in Numbers 21 and Deuteronomy 3.

The first words of the chapter are about age. Joshua is old, and the LORD tells him gently that there is still very much land to be possessed. Then he lists what remains: the regions of the Philistines, the Geshurites, land far to the north toward Lebanon.

The LORD says he will drive these peoples out, and Joshua is told to divide the land among the nine and a half tribes anyway. The chapter then looks back across the Jordan. Moses had already given land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, and the text walks through their borders town by town.

Twice it adds a note about the Levites: they received no land. In one place the text says “The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance”. The work of Joshua’s life is almost finished, yet the chapter admits that it is not all done.

Chapters 13 to 21 describe how the land was shared among the tribes. This chapter sets the stage: it says that parts of the land were still unconquered, and some groups, such as the Geshurites and Maacathites, were not driven out. That sits alongside the language of complete victory earlier in the book, and scholars and readers have long discussed how the two fit together. The Levites’ position is explained in Numbers 18 and Deuteronomy 10.

Caleb is eighty-five years old, and he has been waiting for this day. He steps forward among the people of Judah at Gilgal and reminds Joshua of a promise made forty-five years before. He was forty when Moses sent him to spy out the land, and the men who went with him made the people’s hearts melt. Caleb says, “I wholly followed the LORD my God.”

Moses swore that the land where Caleb had walked would belong to him and his children. Now he asks for the hill country. He speaks of his strength, and he does not pretend the task is easy: the Anakim are there, and the cities are great and fortified. He says it may be that the LORD will be with him.

Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron. The text says it remains his “because he followed the LORD, the God of Israel wholeheartedly.”

The first five verses restate how the land was shared by lot under Eleazar and Joshua. Then the focus narrows to one man. Caleb appears in Numbers 13 and 14, where he and Joshua alone brought back a hopeful report of the land. Hebron already has a long history in the Bible as a place connected with Abraham; see Genesis 23. Caleb is described as a Kenizzite, a detail that suggests his family’s roots were not simple.

This chapter is a map in words. The lot for the tribe of Judah comes first, and the text walks around its edges like a surveyor: south toward Edom and the wilderness of Zin, east along the Salt Sea, north through the valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, and west to the great sea.

In the middle of the borders, one family story appears. Caleb offers his daughter Achsah as a wife to the man who takes Kiriath Sepher. His brother Othniel does it. When Achsah arrives, she asks her father for springs of water, because the land he gave her is dry, and he gives her the upper and the lower springs.

Then come the towns of Judah, grouped by region and counted off. The chapter ends with an admission: the people of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites of Jerusalem, who “live with the children of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.”

Judah’s portion is the largest and is described first, which fits its later place in Israel’s story: David and his kings came from this tribe. The town lists were probably practical records of districts, and scholars debate when they were put in their present form. The story of Achsah and Othniel appears again in Judges 1, and Othniel becomes the first judge in Judges 3. Jerusalem remains outside Israel’s control until the time of David; see 2 Samuel 5.

After Judah comes Joseph, the most numerous of the sons, and his lot is given to his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh together. The chapter starts at the Jordan near Jericho and walks west through the hill country to Bethel, Luz, and on to the sea.

Then it narrows to Ephraim alone. The border lines are listed with their towns, including some towns set apart for Ephraim inside the territory of Manasseh. The reader gets a list of names that were once familiar places to the families who lived there.

The last verse shows the other side of the story: “They didn’t drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer”; Those Canaanites kept living in Ephraim’s land, and the text says they became servants who did forced labor.

Ephraim and Manasseh are the sons of Joseph, adopted by their grandfather Jacob in Genesis 48. The hill country they received was central to Israel’s life, and later the northern kingdom was often called Ephraim. Shiloh, which comes into the next chapters, lay in this territory. The note about Gezer shows a pattern repeated in Judges 1: Israel did not fully take what was promised. See also the summary in Judges 2 of what followed.

Manasseh was Joseph’s firstborn, and his portion is divided in two: Machir’s descendants east of the Jordan, and the rest west of it. Then a family stops the story. Zelophehad had no sons, only five daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. They go to Eleazar the priest, to Joshua, and to the princes and say: “The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers.” They are given land.

The borders of Manasseh follow, and so does a problem. The people could not drive the Canaanites out of their cities, and when Israel grew strong it put them to forced labor instead.

Then the house of Joseph complains that one lot is too small for so many people. Joshua tells them to clear the forest and take the hill country, even though the Canaanites have chariots of iron.

The daughters of Zelophehad first came before Moses in Numbers 27, and their case is settled again in Numbers 36. Here the promise is kept in the land itself, and women are named as heirs, which readers often point out. The complaint of Joseph’s tribes shows that the land was not yet fully secure. Jezreel and Beth Shean were fortified lowland cities; compare the accounts of the fighting there in Judges 1 and 4.

The people gather at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting. The land has been brought under control, but seven tribes still have not received their portion. Joshua asks a sharp question: how long they will “neglect to go in to possess the land”

He asks each of those tribes to choose three men. They are to walk through the land, describe it in a book in seven parts, and bring it back. They go and do exactly that, and Joshua casts lots for them at Shiloh before the LORD.

The rest of the chapter reads the first of those lots: Benjamin gets the narrow strip between Judah and Joseph, running from the Jordan up through the hills. Its borders and its twenty-six towns are listed, including Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon and Jerusalem, called the Jebusite.

Shiloh became the home of the Tent of Meeting for many years, and it comes back in 1 Samuel 1 to 4. Benjamin’s territory was small but sat at a crossroads between Judah and Ephraim, and later King Saul came from this tribe. The survey in this chapter is a rare picture of the land being described and written down before it was divided. Note that Jerusalem is listed here in Benjamin’s territory even though chapter 15 puts its border with Judah; the city is on the line between them.

The lots keep coming at Shiloh. The second falls to Simeon, and its land is found inside the land of Judah, because Judah’s share was too much for them. Then the third lot is for Zebulun, the fourth for Issachar, the fifth for Asher, the sixth for Naphtali, and the seventh for Dan.

Each is described by its borders and towns, in the plain language of a land record. Zebulun and Asher reach toward the sea, Issachar holds the valley of Jezreel, and Naphtali reaches north to Galilee.

The Danites find their land too small, so they go up and fight the town of Leshem and name it Dan, after their forefather. Last of all, the people give Joshua his own inheritance. “According to the LORD’s commandment, they gave him the city which he asked,” Timnath Serah in Ephraim. He builds the city and lives there.

With this chapter the seven remaining tribes receive their land, and the shared task that began in chapter 13 comes to its end. The long lists of names are a record of ordinary places where people would raise families. Scholars debate how the lists reached their present form. The move of Dan to the far north is told more fully in Judges 18. Joshua asks for his own town last, only after everyone else has been served.

A man swings an ax to cut wood, and the head flies off and kills his neighbor. What happens to him? This chapter answers a question like that. The LORD tells Joshua to name cities of refuge, as he had said through Moses.

A man who kills someone accidentally or unintentionally may flee to one of them. He stands at the gate, tells his case to the elders, and they take him in and give him a place to live. If the avenger of blood follows, the city must not hand him over, because he did not hate his neighbor beforehand. He stays until he stands before the congregation for judgment, and until the death of the high priest of those days, and then he may go home.

Six cities are named: three west of the Jordan, Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron, and three east of it, Bezer, Ramoth and Golan. They were for all Israel, and for the foreigner living among them.

The law of the avenger of blood comes from the idea that a family took responsibility for a killing. The cities of refuge give a safe place and a fair hearing between accident and murder. The rules were first given in Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19. The text here is notable for including the foreigner. Christians and Jews have both used the cities of refuge as a picture of God’s mercy; see Hebrews 6 for one New Testament use.

The Levites come forward with a reminder. They were given no land, but the LORD had commanded cities for them to live in, with pasture for their animals. So the tribes give them towns out of their own inheritance, by lot, “as the LORD commanded by Moses.”

The chapter follows the lot family by family. The descendants of Aaron, who are priests, receive thirteen cities in Judah, Simeon and Benjamin. The other Kohathites get ten cities, the Gershonites thirteen, and the Merarites twelve. Six of the towns are named as cities of refuge. In the end the total is stated: forty-eight cities with their pasture lands.

The chapter ends by looking back over the whole conquest. The LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to give, rest on every side, and, in the words of the text, “Nothing failed of any good thing which the LORD had spoken to the house of Israel.”

The Levites had a special role as the tribe set apart for worship and teaching. Scattering them through every tribe meant that no part of Israel was without their care. The command is found in Numbers 35. Some of the towns here are the same ones named in chapter 20 as cities of refuge. The closing summary sounds final, yet the book of Judges that follows shows that the story was not so simple; see Judges 1 and 2.

The fighting is over, and Joshua calls in the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh. They had crossed the Jordan to help their brothers, and he thanks them for keeping every command. He sends them home with a blessing and a charge to love the LORD and hold fast to him.

At the Jordan, those tribes build a great altar. The rest of Israel hears about it and gathers at Shiloh, ready to go to war. First they send Phinehas and ten princes to ask what it means.

The eastern tribes answer with passion: the altar is not for sacrifice. It is a witness for their children, so that in time to come no one on the west will say they have no share in the LORD. Phinehas is pleased. The war that nearly began never happens, and the tribes name the altar “A Witness Between Us that the LORD is God.”

The Jordan was a natural border, and the tribes on the east side feared that later generations would be cut off from the worship at Shiloh. The western tribes feared a repeat of earlier sins at Peor and the trespass of Achan; see Numbers 25 and Joshua 7. The chapter is often read as a story of two sides who talked first and fought later. The worship of the LORD was to be centered at one sanctuary; compare Deuteronomy 12.

Joshua is old, and he knows it. He calls together all Israel, elders, heads, judges and officers, and speaks as someone who is about to go “the way of all the earth.”

He begins by looking back. The LORD has fought for them, and no man has stood before them. Then he turns to what lies ahead. Be very courageous to keep what is written in the book of the law of Moses. Do not mix with the nations that remain, do not mention the name of their gods, and do not marry among them. Hold fast to the LORD, as you have done to this day.

He ends with two promises that are one promise. Every good thing the LORD has spoken has come to pass, and so, if the people go after other gods, will the evil things, until they perish from the good land they were given.

This is the first of Joshua’s two farewell speeches; the second is in chapter 24. Such speeches are a familiar form in the Bible; compare Moses in Deuteronomy 31 and Samuel in 1 Samuel 12. The warning against intermarriage is about worship and loyalty to the LORD, and readers have noted that the Bible elsewhere includes people from outside Israel who joined it, such as Rahab and Ruth. Many scholars link the language of the speech to Deuteronomy.

At Shechem, Joshua gathers all the tribes and begins to tell their story. It starts with Terah, the father of Abraham, who served other gods. It moves through Isaac and Jacob, Egypt, Moses and Aaron, the sea, the wilderness and the Jordan, and it speaks in the voice of the LORD throughout: I took, I gave, I sent, I brought you out.

Then Joshua turns to the people with a choice: “choose today whom you will serve”. He says it plainly: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” The people answer that they will too. Joshua warns them that this is not light, and they say again, “No, but we will serve the LORD.”

Joshua makes a covenant and sets up a great stone under an oak as a witness. Then he dies at one hundred ten, and is buried in his own land. Joseph’s bones, carried from Egypt, are laid to rest in Shechem.

Shechem was a place with deep roots in Israel’s story; Abraham built an altar there, and Jacob bought land nearby (see Genesis 12 and 33). The speech follows the pattern of an ancient treaty, which begins with a history of what the greater king has done. Joshua’s warning that the people cannot serve a holy God lightly has been read in different ways by Jews and Christians. The book ends with a death and a burial, and the story picks up again in Judges 1.
